Senses.Explanation: Telling a dream inside a dream is speech that comments without leaving the condition it describes. Chan masters apply it to teaching distinctions, inherited explanations, and their own words, so the phrase can expose recursive talk without placing the present voice outside it. Chushi Fanqi applies the phrase while sorting inherited explanations. Wuyi Yuanlai extends it to buddhas, patriarchs, old masters, himself, and the assembly in one uninterrupted address. Yanguan Qi’an calls causal color-and-emptiness analysis dream-talk within a dream; Yinyuan Longqi explicitly includes his own address in the same recursive description.

Senses.PreferredTarget: In a dream the six paths appear clear; on waking, the vast world is empty.

Senses.Explanation: Within a dream the six paths of existence seem plainly present; after waking, not even the vast world remains. The pair pivots on a change of standpoint. Poshan and Yinyuan use the contrast to close their own instructions. Dayu claps and laughs before bringing it to the assembly. Guantao has Maitreya speak the pair, then asks whether the words belong to dreaming or waking. Linwo gives it as a direct answer to a question about turning around. The inherited Yongjia verse is recognized as the source of the wording, not counted as five new original compositions.

Senses.Explanation: All that wriggles with spirit — the corpus's one compound for every living being, and the floor the masters lay their claims on: even here, nothing is missing. Huangbo Xiyuan's assembly: mind itself is the buddha — above to the buddhas, below to all that wriggles with spirit, all have buddha-nature, one and the same mind-substance, which is why Bodhidharma came from the west transmitting the one-mind way, pointing straight at every being's already-being-buddha; Wuzu Fayan, settling the stone-Buddha case for his hall, makes his second sample: east Purvavideha a buddha, south Jambudvipa a buddha, west Aparagodaniya a buddha, north Uttarakuru a buddha, grass and trees a buddha, all that wriggles with spirit a buddha — since so, what do you call a sentient being? — and then gives each continent back to itself, gives the grass and trees back to the grass and trees, gives all that wriggles back to all that wriggles: things keep to their own stations, the world's marks abide forever. Pu'an Yinsu's small assembly: all that wriggles with spirit is fully endowed with buddha-nature, fallen into a single dust-grain, unable to awaken itself — only a buddha can know it; yet the great work is done and beings widely converted while deviant lines disorderly make sight and sound, deluding believers, founding buildings and raising images, a hundred kinds of bustle, profit coiling the body like hemp and millet; and Guting Shanjian, giving the precepts to the fourfold assembly: the buddhas' precept wonderfully seals the one mind, all that wriggles with spirit from the start lacks nothing — indeed the whole body of it is the precept, let alone humans and gods — this precept is your one thought of pure mind; outside mind no precept, outside the precept no mind. Mi'an Xianjie, receiving the emperor's incense at the opening of the hall: this is no worldly sandalwood nor overseas eaglewood — where it burns, auspice and omen; mountains, rivers, and the great earth rejoice, all that wriggles with spirit is universally perfumed by right view; and Tianyin Yuanxiu, at the memorial for the layman's father, ladders the seat of settling: know where the departed settles and you know your own; know your own and you know the buddhas' and patriarchs'; know the buddhas' and patriarchs' and you know where all that wriggles with spirit settles — there, buddha and beings are equal, affliction and awakening equal, birth-and-death and quiescence equal, the western quarter and the east equal. Baiyu Jingsi, at the turning of spring: the sun has legs, spreading the great earth's radiance; creation is impartial, the workings of the yang openly shown — sun and moon flower on the unbudding branch, the phoenix dances in the shadowless grove, all that wriggles with spirit is moistened, grass and fiber and mustard all drenched — to know the meaning of buddha-nature, watch the season's cause; the season now come, where is the meaning of buddha-nature? The wooden horse neighs open the moon under the waves, the mud ox ploughs through the smoke on the ridge; and Yushan Shangsi: one leaf falls, heaven and earth autumn; one flower opens, the world arises — the hundred-thousand buddhas turn the root wheel here, the hundred-thousand patriarchs manifest the form-body here, thus mountains and rivers are buddha, grass-mustard and man-and-beast are buddha, scale and feather are buddha, all that wriggles with spirit is buddha.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Kick Mount Sumeru down
Senses.Note: To kick down Mount Sumeru is to overturn the great mountain at the center of the world. Yushan puts the feat in a New Year verse about moving free of sights and sounds. Guxue pairs it with drinking up a river while asking how a ruined monastery recovers its ground. Poshan writes it into a temple poem; Shiyu speaks it at a memorial. Gulin warns that even kicking over Sumeru can leave a person caught in a familiar enclosure. Sanshan says a listener must overturn Sumeru while responding to an old Zhaozhou case. The image tests decisive freedom, but scale by itself is no guarantee of understanding.

Senses.Explanation: When meeting people, speak only three parts; do not give away your whole heart. Use the worldly proverb to check premature disclosure or easy verbal trust. Sanshan Denglai and Shiyu Mingfang use the complete saying in distinct recorded teaching turns. Zhangxue Tongzui, Juelang Daosheng give further current deployments. Chan uses are context dependent; the saying is not a universal command to deceive.

Senses.Note: The masters do not fill in a portable formula for “this way.” Juelang proposes it as an answer about his own teaching. Feiyin uses it after testing the limits of several verbal choices, and Baichi uses it to answer an imagined critic of his poem. Huiyue gives it to a monk who has thanked him; Yushan says it after a monk’s celebratory line. In each setting the listener must answer for the actual encounter when speaking of it to someone else.

Senses.Note: Miyun says this after testing the assembly and finding their response wanting. Baichi says it when a monk cites an old comparison about offerings; Jizong says it after a monk turns a line into a grand claim. Zhe’an says it to a visitor who proposes leaving without formal bowing, and Shending answers a question about circulating the true eye with the warning itself. In each turn it protects the present point from being carried off as a neat second-hand formula. The sources leave the exact thing to be “raised” to the immediate exchange.

Senses.Explanation: One half of the fixed pair of hall sayings from two heirs of the founding teacher's house: meeting someone, I come out; coming out, I do not do it for the person. Xuzhou Pudu raises the pair at his half-mountain seat and rules the two elders one eye and one arm between them, upholding the founding teacher's true line as not two, then sentences both great elders to thirty staff blows, Chijue Daochong raises the pair with the later master's ruling that the two old awls stole scraps of the founder's trade and marked off borders, then faults that ruling itself for knowing one side of two, holding the two elders put out one hand together and broke the founder's line for not a cent, and Xueyan Zuqin raises the pair and snaps it himself, one staff carried by two men and bent into two pieces by the Tianning master, then leans the staff to the left and lets each keep his half. Tianyin Yuanxiu raises the pair with the Xueyan master's verse on it, tells the assembly the verse has scattered the two elders' working to the marrow, and rules that whoever meets it can teach for people or not while whoever does not can neither, Fushi Tongxian gives each elder his season, one bowing to King Wen, one raising arms against Jie and Zhou, then reverses both halves at his Baoen seat, at times coming out and teaching for people, at times not coming out and doing nothing for anyone, and Jiqi Hongchu raises the pair with the Baiyun master's ruling that each elder has one place that lands, weighs the case as not without weight yet unable to escape the Fifth Ancestor grand-teacher's charge of clumsy words, and asks whether the founding teacher's family rule is anything one can bound, carve, or wander loose.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase “Meet a patriarch, kill the patriarch” belongs to Linji’s enumerated formula of killing whatever is encountered, and later masters quote that wording as a sharp inherited command. Literally, "meet a patriarch, kill the patriarch". Linji's surviving record places it inside a five-member roster: "meet buddha, kill buddha; meet a patriarch, kill the patriarch; meet an arhat, kill the arhat; meet parents, kill parents; meet kin, kill kin". This is the Chan bend: the honored religious and familial titles become the grammatical objects of the same repeated verb, and later masters preserve, question, and reuse that severe roster. A successor record explicitly asks why a good teacher would want to kill people after quoting the three religious members, without supplying a prose gloss. Later uses attach the phrase to a sharp sword, place it opposite "carry the infant and encourage the child" in a contrast about grandmotherly kindness, or quote it in a New Year's address before comments on lineage descent. The records use killing language literally in the formula but do not record bodily killings in these uses; this entry adds no symbolic object behind the named roster.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Meet conditions without borrowing
Senses.Note: “Meet conditions without borrowing” describes a response that can move as circumstances change. Zhean applies it to moving among high and low positions; Tianran ties it to a steady source that does not need support from elsewhere, while warning against grasping or license. Weian places it in a compact verse. Tianan links it to giving up Buddha and dharma views. Yunwai sets it against claimed special merit, and Jiqi pairs it with trust in oneself at a memorial. The phrase concerns the source of action, not withdrawal from other people.

Senses.Explanation: On meeting an arhat, kill the arhat is a deliberately violent clause within Linjis escalating instruction to stop depending on any encountered sanctified image. The direct T47 Linji record replaces three parallel recensions of the same speech. Yezhu, Pinjixiang, and Gulin each raise it for distinct current criticism; Liaoan revoices it in his own summer-retreat instruction. The line addresses attachment, not bodily violence. Retained public meaning is supported by independent present uses in recorded discourse.
